title: Standardized Design of Morris Water Maze Experiments and Statistical Analysis
author: Hu, Xu, et al.

steps.title: Open data file in SPSS
steps.instruction: Start SPSS (version 26). Click the ‘Data View’ button and open the original behavioral test file (Data S1) that contains the Morris Water Maze measurements.

steps.title: Define variables in Variable View
steps.instruction: Switch to ‘Variable View’. Create variables named Day1, Day2, Day3, Day4, Day5 for the five training days and factor variables ‘group’ and ‘number’ matching the columns in the data set.

steps.title: Screen and remove outliers
steps.instruction: Open Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Descriptives. Select Day1‑Day5, check ‘Save standardized values as variables’, and click OK. Then filter the newly created ZDay1‑ZDay5 variables and exclude any case whose absolute Z‑score is ≥ 3.

steps.title: Test normality and variance homogeneity
steps.instruction: Open Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Explore. Move Day1‑Day5 to the Dependent List and ‘group’ and ‘number’ to the Factor List. In the Statistics tab, select Descriptives with a 95 % confidence interval for the mean. In the Plots tab, check ‘Factor level together’, ‘Histogram’, and ‘Normality plots with tests’. Click OK to obtain normality test results and Levene’s test for homogeneity of variance.

steps.title: Run repeated‑measures ANOVA with sphericity test
steps.instruction: Open Analyze > General Linear Model > Repeated Measures. In the Define Factor(s) dialog, rename the within‑subject factor to ‘Day’, set Number of Levels to 5, and click Add. Click Define, then move Day1‑Day5 into the Within‑Subjects Variables box and ‘group’ into the Between‑Subjects Factor(s) box. Click Model, choose Type III sum of squares (use Type IV for unbalanced data). Click Plots, set Horizontal Axis = Day, Separate Lines = group, click Add, and display the Day*group interaction. Click Post Hoc, select ‘group’ and check ‘LSD’ for pairwise comparisons. Click Options, set Display Means for ‘Day’, check ‘Compare main effects’, check ‘Descriptive Statistics’, and set the significance level (Alpha) to 0.05. Click OK to run the analysis.

steps.title: Configure post‑hoc LSD comparisons
steps.instruction: In the Post Hoc dialog (accessed from the Repeated Measures procedure), select the factor ‘group’ and tick the ‘LSD’ option to obtain pairwise group comparisons.

steps.title: Set output options and significance level
steps.instruction: In the Options dialog, choose to display means for ‘Day’, compare main effects, include descriptive statistics, and set Alpha = 0.05. Confirm and return to the main GLM window.

steps.title: Execute analysis and generate output tables
steps.instruction: Press OK to run the GLM. SPSS will produce tables including Within‑Subjects Factors, Tests of Within‑Subjects Effects, Tests of Within‑Subjects Contrasts, Tests of Between‑Subjects Effects, Estimates, Descriptive Statistics, and Post Hoc results. Estimated time for this step: 1 h.

steps.title: Interpret sphericity and apply corrections
steps.instruction: Examine Mauchly’s Test of Sphericity. If p > 0.05, sphericity is assumed and the RM‑ANOVA results are used directly. If p < 0.05, apply the Greenhouse‑Geisser or Huynh‑Feldt correction to the degrees of freedom. Note that multivariate tests (Pillai’s Trace, Wilks’ Lambda, Hotelling’s Trace, Roy’s Root) are available and do not require sphericity.

steps.title: Examine within‑ and between‑subject effects
steps.instruction: Review the Tests of Within‑Subjects Effects table for the main effect of Day and the Day × Group interaction. Look at the Within‑Subjects Contrasts to see linear or non‑linear trends across days. Check the Tests of Between‑Subjects Effects for overall group differences independent of time. Consult the Estimates table for adjusted marginal means and 95 % confidence intervals for each group and day.

steps.title: Perform post‑hoc and multivariate tests
steps.instruction: When main or interaction effects are significant, inspect the Pairwise Comparisons and Multiple Comparisons tables. Use the LSD test (or Bonferroni if preferred) to control for multiple testing. Verify robustness by reviewing the multivariate test results (Pillai’s Trace, etc.).

steps.title: Create visualizations of MWM results
steps.instruction: Generate an Estimated Marginal Means plot with Day on the x‑axis, latency on the y‑axis, and separate lines for each group. Produce trajectory plots of animal swim paths for the probe trial on Day 7. Plot escape‑latency curves from Day 2 to Day 6.

steps.title: Report statistical results in manuscript
steps.instruction: Report F values, degrees of freedom, p‑values, effect sizes (η²), and observed power for each significant effect (e.g., F(4,48)=15.99, p<0.001, η²=0.59). Use asterisk notation for p < 0.05. Follow the example format: “RM‑ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of Day … and a significant Day × Group interaction … Post hoc tests indicated that group 3 showed shorter escape latencies than group 1 from Day 3 onward.”

steps.title: Assess spatial and reference memory metrics
steps.instruction: For spatial working memory, examine trajectory plots and line charts of escape latency across Days 2‑6. For reference memory, calculate the time spent in the target quadrant on Day 7 and compare groups (e.g., p < 0.01).

description: The Morris Water Maze (MWM) is widely used to assess hippocampus-dependent spatial learning and reference memory in rodents.1,2 Since the 1980s, it has become a cornerstone assay in neuroscience, behavioral pharmacology, and neuropsychology, used in studies of neurodegenerative diseases, developmental disorders, and antidepressant mechanisms.3,4 The strength of the MWM lies in its reliability across species and laboratories, its independence from food or water restriction, and its ability to capture spatial information during probe trials.5 Despite its ubiquity, MWM data analysis remains inconsistent.6,7 Many studies use simple t-tests at individual time points, neglecting the repeated-measures structure of acquisition data and within-subject correlations.8,9,10 Such approaches increase variability, reduce statistical power, and complicate cross-study comparisons. Probe data analysis also varies, with no clear justification or multiple comparison corrections. Here, we provide a standardized, reproducible IBM SPSS statistical protocol for MWM acquisition and probe data. Acquisition data (e.g., escape latency, path length) are analyzed with repeated-measures analysis of variance (RM-ANOVA) or multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), including assumption testing, sphericity corrections, and post hoc comparisons. Probe outcomes are analyzed with group-level comparisons using parametric or non-parametric methods as appropriate. This protocol is designed to be accessible to researchers with limited statistical background while maintaining rigor and transparency.
